mcqs.question: Why is escaping untrusted data at input time a weaker strategy than escaping at output time?
options: Escaping is computationally expensive and input paths are hotter than render paths
Input escaping cannot handle Unicode, whereas output escaping can
Browsers ignore escaping applied before the value reaches the database
The input path does not know which context the value will be rendered into, and data arriving by other routes never passes through it
mcqs.explanation: The same stored string may later land in HTML, a script block, a URL, an email, or a CSV, and only the renderer knows which encoding applies — plus values from migrations, partner APIs and admin tools reach the renderer without ever crossing the input filter. Cost is not the issue; escaping is cheap in both places.

mcqs.question: A code review shows a user-supplied URL is HTML-entity-encoded before being placed in an `href`. Is that sufficient?
options: Yes — entity encoding neutralises every character that could break out of an attribute
Yes, provided the attribute is wrapped in double quotes
No — entity encoding leaves the URL scheme intact, so a `javascript:` URL still executes on click
No — `href` values must be Base64-encoded before rendering
mcqs.explanation: Entity encoding protects the attribute boundary but does nothing about what the URL means: letters and the colon pass through untouched, so a `javascript:` scheme survives and runs when clicked. The missing control is scheme validation — allow `http:` and `https:` and reject everything else.

mcqs.question:
In React, why can `
{userBio}
` not produce XSS regardless of what `userBio` contains?
options: React renders the value as a text node, so the string is never handed to the HTML parser
React runs DOMPurify over every interpolated value before rendering
React blocks any string containing angle brackets from being rendered
React escapes the value only when it detects a script tag inside it
mcqs.explanation: JSX interpolation creates text, so markup characters are displayed rather than parsed — no filtering or inspection is involved, which is why the value is preserved exactly as typed. React ships no sanitizer of its own; DOMPurify is something you add for the deliberate raw-HTML case.

mcqs.question: Which of these is genuinely still protected by the framework's own sanitizer rather than being a full opt-out?
options: React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`
Vue's `v-html`
Angular's `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml`
Angular's `[innerHTML]` binding
mcqs.explanation: Angular still runs its built-in sanitizer over values bound through `[innerHTML]`, so that path has a real safety net; the explicit `bypassSecurityTrust*` calls are what switch it off. React's and Vue's raw-HTML escape hatches perform no sanitization at all — the value goes straight to the parser.

mcqs.question: Your DOMPurify config allows the `a` tag and the `href` attribute but sets no URI restriction. What is the risk?
options: None — allowing a tag implies its attributes are validated by default
A link whose `href` uses the `javascript:` scheme passes the tag allowlist and executes when clicked
The sanitizer will reject all links, breaking legitimate content
Only that external links will open without `rel="noopener"`
mcqs.explanation: A tag-and-attribute allowlist says which elements survive, not what values are legitimate inside them — so a link with an executable scheme is structurally valid and passes through. That is why `ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP` constraining schemes to http and https is a separate and necessary part of the config.
